issue.title: Eviction claims are piling up in the courts after Section 21 ended
issue.question: More landlords are taking tenants to court since no-fault evictions ended, and the courts are stretched. Who should carry the wait: taxpayers who pay for more courts, landlords, or tenants?
issue.summary: Ministry of Justice figures for July to September 2026 show landlord possession claims in England up 21% to 28,249, with accelerated claims up 68% to a record 12,156. Completed landlord repossessions fell 10% to 6,886. Section 21 no-fault evictions were abolished in England on 1 May 2026, and landlords with valid older notices generally had until 31 July to start court proceedings. The Law Society's president says the courts are not resourced for the increase and warns of continuing backlogs and delays.

bench.title: Ring-fenced landlord claim fee, plus early settlement before court
bench.answer: Keep the county courts and the Section 21 ban. Claims rose 21% to 28,249 and accelerated claims 68% to 12,156 (s1), while the Law Society says courts are under-resourced (s2). The Ministry of Justice would raise the landlord claim fee and ring-fence the money for judges and court staff, so tenants and rent-payers carry no extra cost. Landlords would have to offer a settlement step, such as mediation or a payment plan, before issuing, with the fee refunded if the case settles. Tenants keep full hearings. Check each quarter in the Ministry statistics: median claim-to-possession time (25.9 weeks, s2) should fall while completed repossessions (6,886, s1) do not collapse, and settled cases should rise.

bench.title: Move eviction claims to a dedicated housing tribunal
bench.answer: Possession claims rose 21% to 28,249 in a quarter, with accelerated claims up 68% to a record 12,156 (s1). The Ministry of Justice should move landlord possession claims out of the general courts into a dedicated housing tribunal with its own judges, staff and budget, so other cases stop queuing behind them. It would also run free early mediation for both sides before a hearing. The Law Society says the courts are not resourced for the increase (s2). We would know it worked if completed repossessions, down 10% to 6,886 (s1), recover, waits stay near 25.9 weeks or fall (s2), and the tribunal reports on both.

bench.title: Local settlement desks, paid for by landlords
bench.answer: Claims rose 21% in July to September (s1). In this simulation, landlords would fund local settlement desks through a charge on each rented home, barred from being added to rent. Local tenants and landlords would elect equal numbers to steer each desk and hire independent advisers. Tenants could seek a voluntary payment plan or agreed moving date, with advice of their own. Refusing a deal would not weaken anyone's right to a court hearing. Landlords would carry the financial wait; tenants would stay until lawful eviction. After six months, measure court waiting times, agreements kept and homelessness after cases. Publish the results locally.

jury.question: Who should carry the wait for eviction cases: landlords through a charge, taxpayers through more courts, or should tenants and landlords settle most cases themselves?
options: Landlords pay, through a ring-fenced fee that funds the courts
Taxpayers pay for a separate housing tribunal with its own judges
Local desks steer settlements, paid by a landlord charge
Tenants should not carry any extra cost or risk during the wait
jury.ruling: Landlords pay, through a ring-fenced fee that funds the courts (4 of 12). The jurors who chose it said landlords bring the claims, so landlords should fund the courts that hear them.

reasons.text: Landlords chose to let property and bring the claims. They should fund the courts that hear them.
Taxpayers fund courts for everything else. A separate housing tribunal keeps eviction cases from clogging the rest.
Local desks sound sensible. Most disputes should be settled near home without a judge.
I rent from the council. Whatever happens, renters should not be the ones paying or losing their homes.

minister.trial: In one simulated county court area, for six months, landlords pay a higher claim fee, ring-fenced for extra judge sitting days and court staff there. Landlords must offer mediation or a payment plan before issuing, and the fee is refunded if the case settles. Tenants keep full hearings.
minister.fail_number: If median claim-to-possession time in the trial area is not at least 2 weeks shorter than before, or more than 1 in 10 landlords pass the fee into rent, it has failed.
minister.statement: Claims are up. Courts are full. Somebody has to pay for the extra bench. The jury, twelve simulated jurors, split four, three, two, three, and the biggest group said: landlords pay, and the money goes to judges. So we build exactly that, in one court area. The fee goes on the claim, not on the rent. Every pound is ring-fenced for sitting days. Tenants keep their hearing. Count the weeks. If the wait doesn't shorten, it was a drawing with no stairs.
